title: The Shuttered Wing
logline: When Judith Vane, already promised to Amberlight's curate, is drawn into the mystery of a shuttered wing and a hidden heiress, the very evidence that saves a stranger's inheritance is the thing that very nearly costs Judith her own wedding.
promise: A viewer who came for a gothic mystery gets a disputed inheritance proven by real evidence, a bribe offered in plain sight and flatly refused, and a scandal that burns itself out before the wedding it almost stopped.

cast.name: Miss Judith Vane
cast.station: keeps house for her brother, the apothecary; no fortune of her own
cast.want: To see right done without being bought, bent, or doubted by anyone, in the weeks before her wedding.
cast.appearance: Fair, freckled, of middling height, with reddish hair she cannot keep pinned and a habit of looking directly at whoever is speaking.
cast.dress: Sprigged muslin in summer, a grey wool pelisse in winter, both mended with more thrift than skill.
cast.voice_note: quiet, precise, says less than she thinks

cast.name: Mr Silas Rowe
cast.station: curate of Amberlight; eighty a year and no expectations. Two rooms over Mrs Copp's, looking at the churchyard wall.
cast.want: To protect his parish, and the marriage he has already won, from a scandal neither of them earned.
cast.appearance: Tall and thin, dark hair worn slightly too long, with the stoop of a man used to low doorways and a face that gives away more than he intends.
cast.dress: Worn black coat, carefully brushed, and linen that has been turned at the cuffs.
cast.voice_note: sincere, awkward with anything outside the parish

cast.name: Mr Owen Vane
cast.station: apothecary of Amberlight; modest trade income. Judith's brother and only guardian since their father died.
cast.want: To keep his shop and his sister's good name both unremarked upon.
cast.appearance: Broad-shouldered with his sister's dark colouring, sleeves always rolled to the elbow from the dispensary.
cast.dress: A brown workaday coat and an apron dusted with chalk and powders.
cast.voice_note: dry, blunt, says the thing his sister only thinks

cast.name: Mrs Hale
cast.station: draper's wife; keeps the counter of the circulating library above the shop
cast.want: To be first with every word of a story, and to repeat it exactly as it happened.
cast.appearance: Round-faced and pink, with spectacles pushed up into hair the colour of weak tea.
cast.dress: A striped apron over her gown, never removed even to serve customers upstairs.
cast.voice_note: warm, talks too much, repeats things word for word

cast.name: Mrs Winifred Cardew
cast.station: widow; guardian to her niece and current tenant of the west wing at Amberlight House
cast.want: To secure her niece's inheritance without calling on the parish or inviting its gossip.
cast.appearance: Tall and spare, hair scraped under a widow's cap, with dark hollows beneath her eyes from want of sleep.
cast.dress: A plain grey gown and a single black shawl, kept correct rather than fashionable.
cast.voice_note: guarded, chooses her words as though paying for them

cast.name: Miss Flora Easton
cast.station: granddaughter of the late Sir Edward Marchmont; heiress presumptive to Amberlight House
cast.want: To walk her own grounds openly instead of being kept behind shutters.
cast.appearance: Slight and fair, pale from weeks kept indoors, with quick restless movements and a habit of glancing at doorways.
cast.dress: A plain muslin gown, a little outgrown, with no jewellery at all.
cast.voice_note: hushed and quick, used to being overheard

cast.name: Mr Aubrey Stanhope
cast.station: distant cousin of the late Sir Edward Marchmont; a gentleman of modest independent means, next heir should the marriage in question go unproven
cast.want: To secure the house and its income by whatever means the law, or a willing bribe, allows.
cast.appearance: Compact and dark-haired, smoothly groomed, dressed a shade finer than his means suggest.
cast.dress: A well-cut but slightly dated blue coat and a watch chain he checks too often.
cast.voice_note: smooth, charming, never quite answers the question asked

chapters.title: Lights at Amberlight
beats: The parish already knows Judith Vane and Silas Rowe are promised, their wedding fixed for a date in October, the banns long since read that June.

Word runs along the green that lamps have been seen burning in the long-shuttered west wing of Amberlight House, strange since the east wing has served all summer as the parish schoolroom without any trouble at all.
A closed carriage brings a Mrs Winifred Cardew and her niece, Miss Flora Easton, to the house; they are said to be kin to the late Sir Edward Marchmont, and no more is told.

Rowe calls in his curate's duty to welcome the household and is received briefly by Mrs Cardew, who keeps Flora from the room and asks him not to trouble himself again soon, though he notices a lamp burning behind windows she calls shut up and unused.
He tells Judith that evening, and walking home later herself she sees a light cross behind the shuttered west windows, moving the way no empty room's light has any business doing.

chapters.title: A Letter and a Cousin
beats: Mrs Hale's library counter repeats exactly what Rowe told the sexton about the lamp, and by evening half the green is certain the house is haunted.

Judith receives a letter from her correspondent, Miss Louisa Marchmont, who writes that her uncle, the same gentleman who authorised the schoolroom that summer, acts as Sir Edward's executor, and that the house waits on a question of marriage before any heir can be confirmed.
Owen notes that Mrs Cardew has been buying an unusual quantity of sealing wax and paper from his shop, and seems to be writing to attorneys.

Mr Aubrey Stanhope takes a room at the Bell, calls at Mrs Hale's counter on the pretence of borrowing a volume, and comes away knowing not only of the house but of Judith's own coming wedding, which Mrs Hale is only too pleased to tell anyone who asks.

Stanhope calls at the apothecary shop, introduces himself to Judith as a distant cousin of Sir Edward, and remarks idly that the house cannot pass to anyone until a marriage is proved or disproved, and that he means to see it settled his way before the year is out.

chapters.title: An Errand to the West Wing
beats: Owen, busy with a cough going round the cottages, sends Judith in his place to carry a remedy to Amberlight House, Flora being reported unwell.
Mrs Cardew receives her at the door, anxious and short, and admits only to a legal matter pending that keeps the household wakeful at night.
On the stair Judith glimpses Flora, pale but plainly not sickly, who catches her sleeve and whispers urgently, 'Have you found the prayer,' before Mrs Cardew calls her back.
Leaving in full daylight, Judith looks up at the house and sees the same moving light behind the shuttered west windows, though by every account no one goes there.
That evening Judith tells Rowe everything, and the two agree that someone in that house is hiding something out of fear rather than wrongdoing, and ought to be helped rather than merely watched.

chapters.title: An Offer Refused
beats: Rowe, reading Louisa's letter over again with Judith, works out that Flora must be the granddaughter whose parents' hurried marriage abroad must be proved before she can inherit.
Judith reasons that Mrs Cardew must be searching the house by night for the marriage lines, feared hidden rather than destroyed.
Owen warns Judith that Stanhope has taken to walking past both the shop and the house, asking questions of anyone he meets, and tells her to be wary of him.
Stanhope calls on Judith directly and offers her a comfortable sum toward her and Rowe's household if she will tell him what she finds in the west wing before Mrs Cardew does.
Judith refuses him flatly, offended at the offer, and resolves to find the document herself before Stanhope can ensure it is never found at all.

chapters.title: The Sealed Room
beats: Judith calls on Mrs Cardew, admits what she and Rowe have guessed, and offers her help; worn past pretending otherwise, Mrs Cardew confesses the truth of her fruitless nightly searches and her fear of Stanhope.
Rowe joins them that evening with Mrs Cardew's leave, and Flora is allowed, for the first time in weeks, to help search the rooms that are rightfully to be hers.
In the shuttered west library they find a false-backed cabinet built by Sir Edward's own hand; a portrait comes down as Flora reaches behind it, uncovering a locked strongbox.
The strongbox holds only old letters and a note in Sir Edward's writing, saying he had moved the real proof somewhere 'safer than any lock of mine.'

Unable to force the strongbox's second lock that night, Judith and Rowe step out of the dark house near midnight, and Sarah Copp, sent out on a late errand for her mother, sees the pair leave together and alone.

chapters.title: What Sarah Copp Saw
beats: By morning, Mrs Hale's counter has carried the story the length of the green: the curate and the apothecary's sister, alone in the shut-up house past midnight.
Owen is made uncomfortable before his own customers, who come for the story more than for their physic.
A churchwarden calls on Rowe and asks, gently but plainly, that the wedding be put off until the talk has died down.
Stanhope, hearing the same talk, calls again, not with any offer of marriage but needling Judith that her wedding may not survive the gossip, and repeating his offer of money for the papers.

Lying awake, Judith refuses to be moved by either threat, and turning over Flora's whisper on the stair realizes she misheard 'the paper' for 'the prayer,' and sees where a man who never missed Sunday service would hide what he most wanted kept.

chapters.title: Between Two Boards
beats: At first light Judith brings Rowe a different idea: not the strongbox but Sir Edward's own pew in church, with its locked kneeling-desk nobody had ever thought worth opening.
The village smith is fetched at first light to force the small lock, Mrs Cardew and Flora having come to the church with them.
Folded flat inside the boards of a small prayer book they find the marriage lines from a chapel abroad, signed and witnessed.
Stanhope arrives, having heard where the party went, and argues the lines forged, or at least too late produced to count for anything.
Mrs Cardew answers him by producing a second proof kept separately for years, a witness's letter naming the same marriage and date, and his claim collapses before the two proofs together.

chapters.title: The House Unshuttered
beats: Within days, Louisa Marchmont's uncle, the same gentleman who had authorised the east-wing schoolroom that summer, confirms as executor that Flora is Sir Edward's heir, though she must remain in his keeping as a minor until she comes of age.
Stanhope withdraws his claim without grace and takes the Tuesday coach out of the parish for good.

Mrs Cardew, preparing to take Flora to Bath for the winter, has the west wing's shutters opened at last and gives the west library's shelves to the parish schoolroom to stand alongside the east wing's.
Mrs Hale, delighted the whole business ended so well, declares she always said it would come right, and sets about planning a wedding breakfast nobody has asked her to arrange.
The churchwarden withdraws his objection, and Amberlight church fills for Judith and Rowe's wedding, ending with Judith walking out on her husband's arm as Mrs Rowe.

Character rules:

Setting rules:
- How Judith learns the inheritance question: from a letter from Miss Louisa Marchmont, her correspondent, who writes that her uncle acts as Sir Edward's executor and that the house waits on a question of a marriage. Not from the parish register (it holds baptisms, marriages and burials, not ownership) and not from "old parish papers".
- Louisa's uncle authorised the east-wing schoolroom that June as executor, so his authority must stand. Flora's proved marriage lines make her Sir Edward's heir, but she is under age: the house stays in the executor's keeping until she comes of age. At the end she and Mrs Cardew leave for Bath for the winter, and the west wing's shutters are opened. Nobody takes possession of the main rooms.
- Whoever sees Judith and Rowe leave the dark house late at night is Sarah Copp, Mrs Copp's daughter, who repeats things — not Mrs Pike, who would not be out walking at midnight. They do not go for the Bramdean smith in the night; Bramdean is six miles off. They wait for the village smith at first light.
- The scandal threatens the wedding, not the engagement: a churchwarden asks Rowe to put the wedding off until the talk dies down, and Owen is made uncomfortable before his own customers.
- Do not say where the Rowes will live afterwards, and do not mention a curate's cottage.

Ending: the marriage lines are found in Sir Edward's pew; Stanhope's claim collapses before two proofs; Mrs Cardew gives the west library's shelves to the schoolroom; Mrs Pike plans a wedding breakfast nobody asked her to arrange; the last chapter ends at the wedding itself, in the same church, with Judith walking out as Mrs Rowe.
